In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

in any model with a Higgs sector weakly coupled to the gauge sector, the lightest neutral state is always a Higgs and is always lighter than 1 TeV, with the exception of a small region in the plane of the two Higgs doublet parameters where the Higgs is a pseudoscalar.

the mass of the light scalar in general weakly-coupled Higgs models can be as low as 200 GeV and that the only way to escape such a limit is by having the lightest neutral Higgs state with a large enough coupling to the top quark.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, in general, the mass of the lightest scalar is expected to be at the electroweek scale or below, while heavier scalars are expected to be heavier than the lightest one by an amount controlled by the Higgs self-coupling.

, in general, in any model with an electroweak symmetry breaking sector with arbitrary number of Higgses, there is a neutral Higgs lighter than 1 TeV, and this is the only Higgs which is expected to be produced at the LHC.
in general models with weakly interacting Higgs sector, there always exists a light scalar state with a tree-level mass upper bound of the order of the electroweek scale.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the decoupling of the lightest scalar is not guaranteed in general models, even when all the Higgses have weak couplings to gauge bosons and fermions.
